In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the host odor of cabbage plants, Brassica olearacea, is significantly enhanced in the presence of conspecific larvae.
female diamondback moth responses to host odor are affected by conspecific larvae herbivory but not mating status.
female diamondback moth responses to conspecific larval induced volatiles are more important in host searching, recognition, and acceptance than mating status.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diamondback moth female is a highly sensitive host searcher and is capable of detecting and locating its host plant in the presence of other brassica hosts.
the host searching, recognition and acceptance of gravid female diamondback moth is strongly modulated by conspecific larval feeding on the host plant.
female diamondback moth responses to cabbage host plants are modulated by the presence of conspecific larvae.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the host odor of cabbage plants infested by conspecific larvae is more attractive to gravid female moths than the host odor of intact uninfested hosts.

the presence of conspecific larvae on cabbage host plants can enhance female diamondback moth oviposition and that the use of host plant derived kairomones in monitoring programs for this insect pest may be more useful than the current use of plant derived attractants.
host volatiles are a rich resource for developing new tools and approaches in insect pest management.
